steps.overview: This step builds the LLM basics that every agent depends on: tokens, context windows, sampling settings, chat roles, structured output and core prompting techniques. Agents are LLMs that output decisions such as tool calls, plans and JSON in a loop. If you cannot control what the model outputs and how consistent it is, the agent will break. All four certificates on this path assume this knowledge, and the NCP-AAI and AWS exams test it through scenario questions about reliability and output format.
objectives: Explain tokens, context windows and how input plus output tokens share the model's limit
Describe how temperature and top-p change outputs between runs, and choose settings for agent tasks
Structure a conversation with system, user, assistant and tool messages using a chat template
Produce schema-valid JSON reliably using JSON schemas, constrained decoding and validate-and-retry loops
Apply zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting, and know when each one helps

concepts.explanation: A token is the unit of text the model reads and writes. It can be a whole word, part of a word, a symbol or a space. Each model family has its own tokenizer, so the same text gives different token counts on different models. Cost, latency and context limits are all measured in tokens, not characters or words.

The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can handle in one call. It covers the system prompt, chat history, tool results and the generated output together. When an agent's history grows past this limit, you must trim, summarise or retrieve selectively. A separate max-output-tokens setting limits only the length of the response.

The model gives a probability to every possible next token and then picks one by sampling. Temperature reshapes those probabilities: low values make the output focused and repeatable, high values make it more varied. Top-p (nucleus sampling) keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose combined probability reaches p. This sampling is the main reason the output changes between runs.

Even at temperature 0, outputs can differ slightly between runs. Causes include GPU floating-point effects, request batching on the server and model version updates. Seeds help where the provider supports them, but they rarely guarantee identical output. Design agents to validate their outputs instead of assuming the same output every time.

Chat models take a list of messages with roles: system (rules and persona), user (requests), assistant (past model replies) and tool (tool results, in agent setups). A chat template converts this list into the special-token format the model was trained on. In Hugging Face transformers, tokenizer.apply_chat_template does this conversion. Using the wrong template quietly lowers output quality.

The system prompt sets lasting instructions: role, rules, output format and the tools the model may use. It usually carries more weight than user messages, but it is not a security boundary, because prompt injection can still override it. Keep it specific, put the output-format rules here, and never place secrets in it.

You give the model a JSON schema, and the API or runtime forces the output to match it. This is often done with constrained decoding, where tokens that would break the schema are blocked at each step. Examples include Ollama's format parameter and json_schema response formats. Tool or function calling is the same idea, because the model fills in arguments that follow a schema. Always validate the output in code anyway, for example with Pydantic.

Few-shot prompting puts a few example input-output pairs in the prompt to show the exact format and style you want. It works well for formats that are hard to describe in words. The examples use up context tokens, and the model may copy their quirks. Choose examples that are varied and correct.

Chain of thought asks the model to reason step by step before giving its final answer. It improves accuracy on multi-step problems such as maths, planning and tool selection. In agents, the ReAct pattern alternates reasoning steps with actions. When you need both reasoning and JSON, put the reasoning in a separate field or a separate step so it does not break the JSON.

keyFacts: The context window limit covers input tokens plus output tokens together, so a long prompt leaves less room for the answer.
A common rule of thumb for English is about 4 characters per token, or roughly 3/4 of a word per token. Indian languages and code often use more tokens for the same content.
Low temperature (near 0) suits extraction, classification, JSON and tool calls. Higher temperature suits brainstorming and creative text.
Usually tune temperature or top-p, not both at once.
Temperature 0 does not guarantee identical outputs. Plan for variation and validate every output.
Ranked by how strongly they enforce format: schema-constrained decoding or native structured output, then tool calling, then 'JSON mode' (valid JSON but any shape), then prompt-only instructions.
Always validate model JSON in code and retry with the error message when validation fails. This is the standard reliability pattern.
The Amazon Bedrock Converse API offers one message format across models, with temperature, topP and maxTokens set in inferenceConfig and tools defined via toolConfig.
A stopReason or finish_reason showing the output hit max tokens means the output was cut off. Cut-off JSON is invalid JSON.

example.caption: Hands-on task: get valid, schema-checked JSON for 20 inputs using Ollama structured outputs, Pydantic validation and one retry
example.code:
# pip install ollama pydantic ; then run: ollama pull llama3.1
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError
import ollama

class Ticket(BaseModel):
    category: Literal["billing", "technical", "account", "other"]
    urgency: int  # 1 (low) to 5 (high)
    summary: str

SYSTEM = "Classify the support message. Reply only with JSON matching the schema."
inputs = [f"Sample message {i}: my UPI payment failed twice" for i in range(20)]

def classify(text: str, retries: int = 1) -> Ticket:
    msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": text}]
    for _ in range(retries + 1):
        r = ollama.chat(model="llama3.1", messages=msgs,
                        format=Ticket.model_json_schema(),  # constrained decoding
                        options={"temperature": 0})
        try:
            return Ticket.model_validate_json(r.message.content)
        except ValidationError as e:
            msgs += [{"role": "assistant", "content": r.message.content},
                     {"role": "user", "content": f"Invalid: {e}. Fix it."}]
    raise RuntimeError(f"Failed: {text}")

ok = sum(1 for t in inputs if classify(t))
print(f"{ok}/20 valid")

pitfalls: Thinking temperature 0 makes outputs fully deterministic. Exam scenarios expect you to add validation, retries or constrained decoding, not just lower the temperature.
Using JSON mode and assuming the output matches your schema. JSON mode only guarantees valid JSON syntax; field names and types can still be wrong.
Setting max tokens too low, which cuts the JSON off mid-object. Check finish_reason or stopReason before you parse.
Asking for chain-of-thought reasoning and pure JSON in the same reply, which leaves text around the JSON. Use a 'reasoning' field in the schema or separate the two steps.
Letting chat history grow until it overflows the context window, so the model loses early instructions. Trim or summarise the history, and keep the key rules in the system prompt.
Treating the system prompt as a security control. Untrusted user input or tool output can override it through prompt injection; guardrails are covered in later steps.

workflow.title: How to get reliable structured output from an LLM

steps.label: Define the output schema
steps.detail: Write a Pydantic model or JSON schema with exact field names, types and allowed values (enums).

steps.label: Write system prompt and examples
steps.detail: State the task and format rules in the system message, and add a few varied examples if the format is tricky.

steps.label: Set sampling parameters
steps.detail: Use a low temperature and enough max tokens so the full JSON object fits.

steps.label: Enforce the schema at decode time
steps.detail: Pass the schema through the API's structured output, format or tool-calling feature so invalid tokens are blocked.

steps.label: Validate the response in code
steps.detail: Parse and validate with Pydantic, and check the finish reason for cut-off output.

steps.label: Retry with error feedback
steps.detail: On failure, send the validation error back to the model and ask it to fix the output, with a fixed retry limit.

steps.label: Measure across many inputs
steps.detail: Run a test set such as 20 varied inputs, track the valid-output rate, and adjust the prompt or schema.

objective.question: A model has a 128,000-token context window. Your prompt (system prompt, chat history and documents) uses 125,000 tokens. You ask for a detailed 6,000-token report. What is most likely to happen?
options: The model will automatically summarise the input to make room
The model will raise the context window to fit the request
The output will be cut off or the request rejected, because input and output share the same 128,000-token limit
The model will produce the full 6,000-token report because output tokens are counted separately
objective.explanation: The context window covers input tokens plus output tokens together, so only about 3,000 tokens are left for the answer. Models do not silently summarise the input or grow their window.

objective.question: Using the common rule of thumb for English text, roughly how many tokens is a 2,000-character English paragraph?
options: About 500 tokens
About 8,000 tokens
About 2,000 tokens
About 200 tokens
objective.explanation: The rule of thumb is about 4 characters per token, so 2,000 / 4 ≈ 500 tokens. The other figures assume 10, 1 or 0.25 characters per token.

objective.question: Your team is building a support bot for Hindi and Tamil users. The cost estimate was made from English test data. What risk should you flag?
options: Indian-language text often needs more tokens for the same content, so cost and context use may be higher than estimated
Indian languages cannot be processed by tokenizers at all
Token counts are identical across languages because tokenizers work on meaning
Indian-language text usually needs fewer tokens, so costs will be lower than estimated
objective.explanation: Tokenizers are often trained mostly on English, so Indian scripts usually split into more tokens for the same meaning. This raises cost and fills the context window faster.

objective.question: An agent extracts invoice number, date and amount from emails and returns them as JSON for a downstream system. Which temperature setting is the best starting point?
options: Around 1.0
Temperature does not matter for extraction
Around 1.5
Near 0
objective.explanation: Low temperature makes the model choose high-probability tokens, which suits extraction, classification, JSON and tool calls. High temperatures add randomness that suits creative tasks, not strict formats.

objective.question: A developer sets temperature to 1.4 and top-p to 0.2 in the same request and cannot understand why output quality keeps changing in odd ways. What is the best advice?
options: Usually tune either temperature or top-p, not both at once, so you can see the effect of each change
Top-p only affects output length, so ignore it
Set top-p to 0 to make temperature work
Always set both to their maximum values
objective.explanation: Both settings control sampling randomness, and changing both at once makes their combined effect hard to predict and debug. Top-p limits the pool of candidate tokens; it does not control length.

objective.question: You set temperature to 0 and send the same prompt twice. The two responses differ slightly. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Temperature 0 does not guarantee identical outputs, so the system should validate outputs and tolerate variation
Temperature 0 only applies to the first token
The prompt must contain a hidden random seed
The API is broken and should be reported
objective.explanation: Even at temperature 0, things like floating-point effects, batching and serving infrastructure can cause small differences. The right design plans for variation and validates every output.

objective.question: Which method gives the strongest guarantee that a model's output will match a specific JSON schema?
options: JSON mode
Schema-constrained decoding or native structured output
Tool calling with a defined input schema
Writing 'Return only JSON' in the system prompt
objective.explanation: From strongest to weakest: schema-constrained decoding or native structured output, then tool calling, then JSON mode, then prompt-only instructions. Constrained decoding limits which tokens can be generated so that they fit the schema.

objective.question: You enable 'JSON mode' on a model. Your parser keeps failing with errors like 'missing field: amount'. Why?
options: JSON mode only works at high temperature
JSON mode always removes numeric fields
JSON mode returns XML instead of JSON
JSON mode guarantees valid JSON syntax but not a particular shape or set of fields
objective.explanation: JSON mode makes the output parse as JSON, but it can be any shape. To enforce required fields you need schema-constrained output or tool calling, plus validation in code.

objective.question: A Bedrock Converse API call returns stopReason 'max_tokens' and your JSON parser fails. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The output was cut off at the token limit; raise maxTokens or ask for shorter output, then validate again
The guardrail blocked the content; remove the guardrail
The temperature is too low; raise it to 1.0
The model refused the request; rephrase it politely
objective.explanation: A max_tokens stop reason means generation stopped at the output limit, and cut-off JSON is invalid JSON. Raising the limit or reducing output size fixes it. Temperature and politeness are not related.

objective.question: In the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, where do you set temperature, topP and maxTokens?
options: In inferenceConfig
In a model-specific body field that differs for every provider
In the system message text
In toolConfig
objective.explanation: Converse uses one common format across models, and sampling settings go in inferenceConfig. toolConfig is for defining tools, and the system prompt is for instructions, not parameters.

objective.question: You want a Bedrock model to return customer data in a fixed structure by 'calling' a function with typed parameters. Using the Converse API, how do you define that function?
options: Via inferenceConfig.temperature
Via the stopSequences setting
By pasting the function's source code into the user message
Via toolConfig, with a tool specification that includes a JSON schema for its input
objective.explanation: Tools are defined in toolConfig, and each tool has an input schema that the model's arguments must follow. This is a common way to get structured output. The other options do not define tools.

objective.question: Users of your chatbot keep changing its persona by typing 'You are now a pirate'. Where should the rules about persona and allowed behaviour live, and why?
options: In the system prompt, because it sets persistent instructions that the model is trained to weight above ordinary user turns
In the assistant message, because the model trusts its own words
In inferenceConfig, because it is a parameter
In the first user message, because models read user text first
objective.explanation: The system prompt holds the developer's standing instructions and has higher priority than user turns. It is not perfect protection, though, so sensitive rules still need checks in code and guardrails.

objective.question: A classifier must label support tickets into 6 company-specific categories with subtle differences. Zero-shot results confuse 'billing dispute' with 'refund request'. What is the most effective next step in the prompt?
options: Remove the category definitions to reduce tokens
Ask the model to reply in a single word without instructions
Add a few labelled examples, including ones that show the billing-versus-refund boundary
Raise temperature so the model explores more labels
objective.explanation: Few-shot examples show the model the exact pattern and boundary cases you want, which often fixes confusion between similar labels. Raising temperature adds randomness, and removing definitions takes away useful context.

objective.question: A task benefits from step-by-step reasoning, but the application needs strict JSON with a final 'decision' field. Which design is best?
options: Add a 'reasoning' field that comes before 'decision' in the schema, so the model reasons first and then answers, and validate the result
Forbid all reasoning because chain of thought always breaks JSON
Set temperature to 2 so the model thinks harder
Ask for reasoning in free text mixed into the JSON values
objective.explanation: Models generate tokens in order, so placing a reasoning field before the decision lets the reasoning shape the answer while the output stays valid JSON. Mixing free text into values breaks parsing, and temperature does not create reasoning.

objective.question: Your pipeline sends 10,000 documents to an LLM for structured extraction. About 2% of responses fail schema validation. What is the standard reliability pattern?
options: Switch off validation to improve throughput
Increase temperature on every request so the model avoids repeating mistakes
Validate each output in code, then retry with the validation error message included in the prompt, up to a retry limit
Accept the bad records and fix them by hand later
objective.explanation: Validate, then retry with the specific error, is the standard pattern. The error message tells the model exactly what to fix, and a retry cap stops endless loops. Raising temperature makes format errors more likely, not less.

subjective.question: Why does an LLM's output change between runs, even with the same prompt?
subjective.answer: An LLM generates text one token at a time. At each step it produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens, and then a token is sampled from it. With temperature above zero, lower-probability tokens can be chosen, and one different early token changes everything that follows. Even at temperature 0, outputs are not guaranteed to be identical. Floating-point arithmetic, batching with other requests on the GPU, and changes in the serving setup can shift probabilities slightly, and near-ties can flip. Model versions can also be updated behind the same name. So I treat outputs as variable by design. I lower temperature for deterministic tasks, constrain the format, and validate every response in code rather than assume consistency.
keyPoints: Token-by-token sampling from a probability distribution
Temperature and top-p add randomness; early differences compound
Temperature 0 is not a guarantee: floating point, batching, infrastructure
Model version changes
Design for variation: constrain and validate

subjective.question: How would you constrain a model's output so that a downstream system can trust it?
subjective.answer: I layer several controls. First, I use the strongest format enforcement available. That means schema-constrained decoding or native structured output if the model supports it, otherwise tool calling with an input schema, then JSON mode, and prompt-only instructions as the last resort. Second, I set temperature near 0 for extraction or classification. Third, I write a clear system prompt with field definitions, allowed values and a few examples. Fourth, I set maxTokens high enough and check the stop reason so that truncated output is caught. Finally, and most importantly, I validate every response in code against the schema and business rules. On failure I retry with the error message, up to a limit, and log the failures I cannot fix. No single control is enough on its own.
keyPoints: Format enforcement ranking: constrained decoding > tool calling > JSON mode > prompt
Low temperature for deterministic tasks
Clear system prompt with examples
Check stop reason for truncation
Validate in code and retry with the error

subjective.question: What is a token, and why should an engineer care about token counts?
subjective.answer: A token is the unit a model actually reads and writes. It is usually a piece of a word, a whole short word, punctuation, or a chunk of code. For English, a common rule of thumb is about 4 characters per token, or roughly three quarters of a word. Token counts matter for three practical reasons. First, cost: most APIs bill per input and output token. Second, limits: the context window and max output are measured in tokens. Third, latency: more output tokens means a slower response. Indian languages and code often need more tokens for the same content, so estimates based on English can be badly wrong. In real work I measure with the model's own tokenizer, or use the token usage the API returns, instead of guessing.
keyPoints: Token is a sub-word unit
About 4 characters or 3/4 of a word per token in English
Drives cost, context limits and latency
Indian languages and code use more tokens
Measure with the real tokenizer or API usage

subjective.question: Explain the context window and how you would budget it in a RAG chatbot.
subjective.answer: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can handle in one request, and it covers input plus output together. In a RAG chatbot the input includes the system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved chunks, chat history and the user's question. Whatever is left is the room for the answer. I budget explicitly. I reserve output tokens first using maxTokens. I keep the system prompt tight. I cap the number and size of retrieved chunks. I trim or summarise old chat history. If I skip this, a long history slowly eats the space, and answers get cut off or the request fails. I also remember that a larger window does not mean better use of it: models can miss details buried in very long contexts. So relevant, shorter context usually beats stuffing everything in.
keyPoints: Window covers input plus output
List the parts: system, tools, retrieved docs, history, question
Reserve output first; cap retrieval; trim history
Truncation or failure if over budget
More context is not always better

subjective.question: Compare temperature and top-p. When would you use which settings?
subjective.answer: Both control how random token sampling is. Temperature reshapes the probability distribution. Low values sharpen it so the top tokens dominate; high values flatten it so less likely tokens get picked more often. Top-p, or nucleus sampling, keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose combined probability reaches p, and then samples from that set. A low top-p cuts off the long tail. For extraction, classification, JSON and tool calls I use low temperature, near 0. For brainstorming, marketing copy or story ideas I raise it. My usual practice is to tune one of them and leave the other at its default. Changing both makes the effect hard to reason about and hard to debug. Whichever I choose, I compare outputs on a fixed test set before shipping.
keyPoints: Temperature reshapes the distribution
Top-p limits the candidate pool by cumulative probability
Low for structured tasks, higher for creative ones
Tune one, not both
Evaluate on a test set

subjective.question: Describe the roles in a chat message format and how a multi-turn conversation is actually sent to the model.
subjective.answer: Chat APIs use a list of messages, each with a role. The system role holds the developer's standing instructions: persona, rules, output format. The user role holds the human's input. The assistant role holds the model's earlier replies. With tool use, there are also tool calls and tool results, which in the Bedrock Converse API appear as content blocks such as toolUse and toolResult. The key point is that the model is stateless. It does not remember the earlier turns of a conversation. On each turn, the application resends the full relevant history. This is why long chats get more expensive and eventually hit the context window. It is also why the application must manage history by trimming, summarising or storing memory. That idea leads directly to agent memory later in this course.
keyPoints: System, user and assistant roles, plus tool messages
System holds persistent developer instructions
Model is stateless; history is resent each turn
Cost and context grow with history
Application manages memory

subjective.question: What makes a good system prompt for a production extraction task?
subjective.answer: A good system prompt is specific, structured and testable. I start with the role and the task in one or two lines. Then I define every output field: its meaning, type, format such as ISO dates, and allowed values. I state clearly what to do when information is missing, for example return null, and say never to guess. I add a few examples, including tricky edge cases. I separate instructions from untrusted input using clear delimiters, and I tell the model to treat document content as data, not instructions. That reduces prompt-injection risk. I avoid vague words like 'be accurate' and use concrete rules instead. Finally, I version the prompt and run it against a fixed test set whenever I change it, because small wording changes can shift behaviour.
keyPoints: Role and task stated clearly
Field definitions, types, allowed values
Explicit missing-data rule: null, not guessing
Examples and delimiters for untrusted input
Version and regression-test the prompt

subjective.question: Explain the difference between JSON mode, tool calling and schema-constrained structured output.
subjective.answer: All three aim at machine-readable output, but they enforce it with different strength. JSON mode makes the model produce syntactically valid JSON, but it can be any shape. Fields can be missing, renamed or of the wrong type. Tool calling lets you define a tool with a JSON schema for its input. The model returns arguments meant to fit that schema, which usually gives good shape adherence, and it is also how agents take actions. Schema-constrained decoding, or native structured output, is the strongest. The decoder only allows tokens that keep the output valid against the schema, so the structure is guaranteed within the supported schema features. Prompt-only instructions are the weakest. Even with the strongest option I still validate in code, because a schema cannot check business rules like 'amount must match the line items'.
keyPoints: JSON mode: valid syntax, any shape
Tool calling: schema-guided arguments; basis of agents
Constrained decoding: strongest guarantee
Prompt-only is weakest
Still validate business rules in code

subjective.question: Design a validate-and-retry loop for LLM JSON output. What details matter?
subjective.answer: After each call, I first check the stop reason. If it shows max tokens, the output was cut off, and cut-off JSON is invalid JSON. So I raise the limit or ask for less output, rather than blindly retrying. Next I parse the JSON, then validate it against the schema with a library such as Pydantic or jsonschema. Then I check business rules. If anything fails, I retry with the original messages plus the model's bad output and the exact error message, for example 'field amount must be a number', and ask it to correct only that. I cap retries at two or three, use backoff for API errors, and send permanent failures to a dead-letter queue for review. I log failure rates per prompt version, because a rising rate signals a prompt or model change.
keyPoints: Check stop reason for truncation first
Parse, then schema-validate, then check business rules
Retry with the specific error message
Cap retries; dead-letter queue
Monitor failure rates

subjective.question: Walk through how you would complete the hands-on task: get a model to return valid JSON for 20 different inputs.
subjective.answer: First I define a JSON schema, for example for extracting name, city, product and sentiment from customer messages, with types, required fields and enums. Then I build 20 varied inputs: short, long, Hindi-English mixed, missing fields, sarcastic, and one with an injection attempt like 'ignore instructions'. I write a system prompt with field rules and two examples, and set temperature near 0. I use native structured output or a tool schema if available, otherwise JSON mode. In code, I check the stop reason, parse the output, and validate it against the schema, retrying with the error on failure. I record first-try pass rate, final pass rate and retries for each input. Then I improve the prompt from the failures. I run the whole set more than once, because outputs vary between runs.
keyPoints: Define the schema first
Diverse inputs, including edge cases and injection
Low temperature; strongest format option
Validate and retry with metrics
Run multiple times; iterate on failures

subjective.question: What happens when output is truncated, and how do you detect and prevent it?
subjective.answer: Truncation happens when generation hits the max output tokens limit, or when the context window runs out, before the model finishes. The response just stops mid-sentence or mid-object. For JSON that is serious, because a missing closing brace makes the whole thing invalid. To detect it, I check the stop reason every time. In the Bedrock Converse API, stopReason is max_tokens; in OpenAI-style APIs, finish_reason is 'length'. I do not rely only on the parser failing. To prevent it, I set maxTokens with headroom for the largest expected output, keep the input budget under control, and design outputs to be compact: short keys, and no unnecessary prose or reasoning fields when they are not needed. For large lists, I paginate or split the task into chunks rather than ask for everything at once.
keyPoints: Caused by max tokens or context limit
Cut-off JSON is invalid
Check stopReason max_tokens or finish_reason length
Set maxTokens with headroom
Compact outputs; chunk large tasks

subjective.question: When does few-shot prompting help, and what are its pitfalls?
subjective.answer: Few-shot prompting means adding example input-output pairs to the prompt. It helps most when the task has a specific format, custom labels, a particular tone, or subtle boundaries that are hard to describe in words. One good example of a tricky case can beat a paragraph of rules. There are pitfalls. Examples cost tokens on every call. Models can copy the examples too closely, reusing their wording or values, or skewing towards the most common label in the examples. Examples that contradict the instructions confuse the model. Poorly chosen examples that are all easy cases do not teach the edges. My practice is to use a small number of diverse, correct examples that cover boundary cases, keep them consistent with the schema, and check on a test set that they really improve results.
keyPoints: Best for custom formats, labels, subtle boundaries
Token cost on every call
Risk of copying examples and label bias
Examples must match the instructions and schema
Use diverse boundary cases; measure the impact

subjective.question: What is chain-of-thought prompting? When is it useful, and when should you avoid it?
subjective.answer: Chain of thought means getting the model to work through intermediate steps before giving the final answer. You can ask it to think step by step, show worked examples, or use a model with built-in reasoning. Because tokens are generated in order, reasoning written first can improve the answer that follows. It helps for multi-step maths, logic, planning and complex classification. I avoid or limit it for simple extraction or high-volume tasks, because it adds tokens, cost and latency, and it can make it harder to parse the output. When I need both reasoning and strict output, I put a reasoning field before the answer field in the schema, or use a separate step. I also remember that the stated reasoning is not a guaranteed true explanation of how the model decided, so I still verify the final result.
keyPoints: Intermediate steps before the answer
Helps multi-step reasoning and planning
Costs tokens and latency; skip for simple tasks
Reasoning field before answer for structured output
Reasoning text is not guaranteed faithful; verify

subjective.question: Why might a team use the Amazon Bedrock Converse API instead of model-specific request formats?
subjective.answer: The Converse API gives one consistent message format across the models on Bedrock. So the same code can call different providers' models, and swapping models for cost or quality comparison becomes a configuration change instead of a rewrite. Messages use roles and content blocks. The system prompt is a separate field. Sampling settings such as temperature, topP, maxTokens and stop sequences go in inferenceConfig. Tools are defined in toolConfig with JSON input schemas, which supports structured output and agent actions. The response includes a stopReason, such as end_turn, tool_use or max_tokens, and token usage, which helps with truncation handling and cost tracking. One caveat: not every model supports every feature, such as tool use or certain content types, so I check feature support for each model before switching.
keyPoints: One format across models; easy model swaps
Separate system field and role-based messages
inferenceConfig for temperature, topP, maxTokens
toolConfig for tools with schemas
stopReason and usage returned; check per-model feature support

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: 'We set temperature to 0, so our LLM pipeline is deterministic and doesn't need tests.' How do you respond?
subjective.answer: I would politely disagree. Temperature 0 reduces randomness, but it does not guarantee identical outputs. GPU floating-point effects, request batching and infrastructure changes can shift results slightly. Providers may also update models behind the same name. And even a fully deterministic model can be consistently wrong, or fail on inputs it has never seen, so testing is about correctness, not only consistency. I would propose three things. First, schema validation and business-rule checks on every production output, with retry and a fallback path. Second, a fixed evaluation set run on every prompt or model change, with metrics such as validity rate and accuracy. Third, monitoring of failure rates in production. Pinning a specific model version where possible also helps. Determinism is a nice-to-have; validation is the requirement.
keyPoints: Temperature 0 is not a guarantee
Model updates change behaviour
Consistency is not correctness
Validate every output; regression eval set
Monitor production; pin model versions

steps.overview: This step teaches how a language model uses external functions. You describe a tool with a name, a description and a JSON Schema. The model asks for a call, your code runs it, and you send the result back. That loop sits inside every agent framework, including smolagents, LangGraph, NVIDIA NeMo Agent Toolkit and Amazon Bedrock Agents. All four certificates on this path test it, often as scenarios about wrong tool selection, malformed arguments, parallel calls and error handling.
objectives: Write tool definitions with a clear name, a precise description and a valid JSON Schema for the inputs.
Implement a complete tool-calling loop by hand that detects tool requests, runs the tools and returns results with matching IDs.
Handle parallel tool calls and tool errors so the model can recover instead of the program crashing.
Explain the Model Context Protocol (MCP) architecture and how tools/list and tools/call expose tools in a standard way.
Map each part of the manual loop to what a framework (smolagents, LangGraph, Bedrock Agents) does for you automatically.

concepts.explanation: A tool is declared to the model as a name, a natural-language description and an input schema written in JSON Schema. The model never sees your code. It sees only this declaration, so the description decides when the model picks the tool and the schema decides what arguments it produces. In the Anthropic API the field is input_schema. In the OpenAI API it is function.parameters. In the Bedrock Converse API it is toolSpec.inputSchema.json.

You send the user message plus the tool definitions. The model replies with a tool-use request (Anthropic stop_reason 'tool_use'; OpenAI finish_reason 'tool_calls'). Your code runs the function and appends the result to the conversation, then calls the model again. This repeats until the model returns a normal text answer. The model only proposes calls; your application always executes them.

concepts.term: Tool call ID and tool result
concepts.explanation: Every tool request carries a unique ID, and the result you send back must reference that same ID. In Anthropic's API this is a tool_result block with tool_use_id inside a user message. In OpenAI's API it is a message with role 'tool' and tool_call_id. A missing or mismatched ID causes an API validation error or a confused model.

A model can request several independent tools in one turn, for example the weather and a calculation together. You should run all of them, concurrently if possible, and return every result. In Anthropic's API all tool_result blocks go together in a single user message. Parallel calls cut round trips and latency, but they only make sense for tasks that do not depend on each other.

When a tool fails, catch the exception and return the error text as the tool result, flagged as an error where the API supports it (Anthropic is_error: true, Bedrock status 'error'). The model can then retry with fixed arguments, choose another tool or explain the problem. An unhandled exception ends the agent run, and silently dropping a result breaks the message sequence.

This setting controls whether the model must use tools. Anthropic supports auto, any, a specific tool, and none. OpenAI supports auto, required, none, or a named function. Forcing a tool is useful for structured extraction. Leaving it on auto lets the model answer directly when no tool is needed.

MCP is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic, that standardises how applications expose tools and context to models. A host (such as Claude Desktop or an IDE) runs one MCP client per server. Clients and servers exchange JSON-RPC 2.0 messages over stdio for local servers or Streamable HTTP for remote ones. Clients discover tools with tools/list and run them with tools/call, so one server works with any MCP-compatible agent.

Servers expose three primitives: tools (actions the model can invoke), resources (read-only data the application can load as context) and prompts (reusable templates the user picks). Clients can offer features back to servers, such as sampling (the server asks the host's model for a completion), roots and elicitation. Exam questions often check that you can tell tools (model-controlled) apart from resources (application-controlled).

keyFacts: The model never executes code. It returns a structured request, and your application runs the tool and returns the result.
A tool definition has three parts: name, description and input schema (JSON Schema, usually type 'object' with properties and required).
Anthropic: check stop_reason == 'tool_use', read the tool_use blocks (id, name, input), and reply with tool_result blocks that carry tool_use_id.
OpenAI: function arguments arrive as a JSON string that you must parse; results are sent back as role 'tool' messages with tool_call_id.
Bedrock Converse API: tools go in toolConfig.tools[].toolSpec, stopReason is 'tool_use', and results are toolResult blocks with an optional status of 'error'.
Always cap the loop with a maximum number of iterations to prevent infinite tool-calling cycles and runaway cost.
MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0. Its standard transports are stdio (local) and Streamable HTTP (remote), which replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport in the 2025 spec.

Hugging Face smolagents provides ToolCallingAgent (JSON tool calls) and CodeAgent (actions written as Python code). Its @tool decorator builds the schema from type hints and the docstring's Args section.
Bedrock Agents define tools as action groups, described by an OpenAPI schema or function details, usually backed by a Lambda function.

pitfalls: Writing vague tool descriptions such as 'weather tool'. The model picks tools from their descriptions, so say what the tool does, when to use it and what each argument means.
Forgetting to append the assistant's tool-use turn before the tool results. The API expects the full sequence: assistant tool request, then user tool result.
Splitting parallel results across several messages, or returning only some of them. Every tool request needs exactly one result with the matching ID.
Letting tool exceptions crash the loop or hiding them. Return the error as a tool result so the model can recover.

Running model-generated arguments without checks, for example calling bare eval or SQL on them. Validate inputs against the schema and apply least privilege, because tool inputs can be prompt-injected.
Assuming MCP replaces function calling. MCP standardises how tools are discovered and served; the model still uses its API's normal tool-calling mechanism underneath.

objective.question: A product manager says, 'Our LLM called the weather API and got the forecast.' In a standard tool-calling setup, what actually happened?
options: The model returned a structured request naming the tool and its arguments, and the application ran the tool and sent the result back
The model looked up the forecast in its training data and formatted it as a tool call
The model generated Python code that the provider automatically executed in a sandbox
The model sent an HTTP request to the weather API from the provider's servers
objective.explanation: In client-side tool calling, the model never executes anything. It only emits a structured tool request, and your code runs the tool and returns the result. Provider-run sandboxes and training-data recall are not how custom tool calling works.

objective.question: Which three parts make up a tool definition that you send to a model?
options: Function body, return type and timeout
Description, example output and retry policy
Name, description and input schema
Name, endpoint URL and API key
objective.explanation: A tool is described by a name, a natural-language description and an input schema written in JSON Schema. The model never sees endpoints, keys or the function body.

objective.question: You call the Anthropic Messages API with a get_weather tool. The response has stop_reason 'tool_use' and a tool_use block with id 'toolu_01A', name 'get_weather' and input {"city":"Pune"}. What should your next request contain?
options: The original messages, the assistant turn with the tool_use block, then a user message with a tool_result block whose tool_use_id is 'toolu_01A'
A message with role 'tool' and tool_call_id 'toolu_01A'
A system message with the weather result and no assistant turn
A new user message with plain text saying 'The weather in Pune is 31°C'
objective.explanation: Anthropic expects the assistant's tool_use turn to stay in the history, followed by a user message holding a tool_result block linked by tool_use_id. A role 'tool' message is the OpenAI format, not Anthropic's.

objective.question: Using OpenAI Chat Completions, a developer writes city = tool_call.function.arguments['city'] and gets a TypeError. What is the most likely cause?
options: function.arguments is a JSON string and must be parsed, for example with json.loads, before reading keys
The tools parameter must be set to strict mode to return arguments
Tool arguments are only available after you send a role 'tool' message
The model did not include the city argument
objective.explanation: OpenAI returns function arguments as a JSON-encoded string, so you have to parse it first. Indexing a string with a key raises a TypeError. The other options do not explain this specific error.

objective.question: A user asks, 'What is the weather in Delhi and Chennai?' The model returns two tool calls in one turn. What is the correct way to handle this?
options: Run both calls (in parallel if you can) and return both results in the next turn, each linked to its own call ID
Merge both results into one string and attach it to the first call ID
Reject the turn, because models can only make one tool call at a time
Run only the first call, return its result and wait for the model to ask again
objective.explanation: With parallel tool calls, every call needs its own result, matched by its ID, and all results are returned together in the next turn. Dropping one call or merging results under one ID breaks the pairing, and the APIs will usually reject it.

objective.question: Your weather tool throws an exception because the city 'Bombay Central' is not found. What is the recommended way to handle it inside the agent loop?
options: Return a tool result that describes the error and mark it as an error (for example, is_error in Anthropic or status 'error' in Bedrock) so the model can retry or explain
Retry the same call forever until it succeeds
Silently skip the tool result and call the model again
Crash the loop and show a stack trace to the user
objective.explanation: Treating errors as observations lets the model change its arguments, try another tool or tell the user what went wrong. Crashing, skipping the result or retrying forever all break the loop or waste cost.

objective.question: In testing, an agent keeps calling a search tool with slightly different queries and never gives a final answer, which runs up a large token bill. What is the most important safeguard to add to a hand-written loop?
options: A maximum number of loop iterations, after which the loop stops and returns a fallback answer
Removing the tool description, so the model uses the tool less
A higher temperature, so the model explores more
A higher max_tokens value
objective.explanation: An iteration cap prevents infinite tool-calling cycles and runaway cost. Raising max_tokens or temperature does nothing to end the loop, and removing the description makes tool use worse.

objective.question: You want the model to call one of your tools on every turn, but let it choose which one. Which tool_choice setting does this?
options: OpenAI 'none' / Anthropic 'none'
OpenAI 'required' / Anthropic 'any'
Naming one specific function, on both APIs
OpenAI 'auto' / Anthropic 'auto'
objective.explanation: OpenAI 'required' and Anthropic 'any' force a tool call but leave the choice of tool to the model. 'auto' lets the model skip tools, 'none' blocks them, and naming a function forces that single tool.

objective.question: You are moving tool calling to the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. Where do you put the calculator tool definition?
options: In toolConfig.tools[].toolSpec, with name, description and inputSchema.json
In a system prompt block written as JSON
In the tools[].function field, as OpenAI does
In actionGroups[].apiSchema of the Converse request
objective.explanation: Converse takes tools in toolConfig.tools[].toolSpec, and the JSON Schema goes under inputSchema.json. Action groups belong to Bedrock Agents, not Converse. tools[].function is the OpenAI shape.

objective.question: Your team is deploying an MCP server as a shared remote service for many clients over the network. Which standard transport should it use under the current spec?
options: HTTP+SSE (the original two-endpoint transport)
gRPC streaming
Streamable HTTP
stdio
objective.explanation: Streamable HTTP is the standard remote transport, and it replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport in the 2025 spec. stdio is meant for local subprocess servers, and gRPC is not a standard MCP transport.

objective.question: An MCP client has connected to a server and finished initialisation. It now wants to find out which tools the server offers. Which JSON-RPC method does it call?
options: tools/call
initialize
resources/read
tools/list
objective.explanation: tools/list returns the tool names, descriptions and input schemas. tools/call runs a tool, resources/read fetches resource content, and initialize is the earlier handshake.

objective.question: An MCP server needs to expose read-only project files that the host application can attach as context. The model should not invoke them as actions. Which MCP primitive fits best?
options: Resources
Prompts
Sampling
Tools
objective.explanation: Resources expose data, such as file contents, for the application to provide as context. Tools are model-invoked actions, prompts are reusable templates usually chosen by the user, and sampling lets a server ask the client for a model completion.

objective.question: In smolagents, a developer decorates a function with @tool but the agent fails to build the tool's schema. The function has type hints but only a one-line docstring. What is most likely missing?
options: An Args section in the docstring that describes each parameter
An OpenAPI file next to the function
A class that inherits from ToolCallingAgent
A return statement that returns JSON
objective.explanation: The @tool decorator builds the schema from the type hints and the docstring, and it needs an Args section that describes each argument. The other options are not requirements of @tool.

objective.question: Which statement correctly contrasts smolagents' CodeAgent with its ToolCallingAgent?
options: ToolCallingAgent runs code in a sandbox; CodeAgent never executes anything
They are the same class under two names
CodeAgent can only use built-in tools; ToolCallingAgent can use custom tools
CodeAgent writes its actions as Python code snippets that are executed; ToolCallingAgent emits JSON-style tool calls
objective.explanation: CodeAgent expresses actions as Python code, which can chain several tool calls and some logic in one step. ToolCallingAgent uses structured JSON tool calls. Both can use custom tools.

objective.question: A team builds an Amazon Bedrock Agent that must look up order status in an internal system. Which setup matches how Bedrock Agents define and run tools?
options: Create an action group described by an OpenAPI schema or function details, usually backed by a Lambda function that runs the lookup
Upload the order database as a knowledge base, which runs the queries automatically
Register the tool as a guardrail policy
Add the tool to toolConfig in every Converse call
objective.explanation: Bedrock Agents expose tools as action groups, defined with an OpenAPI schema or function details and usually fulfilled by Lambda. Knowledge bases handle retrieval, guardrails handle safety, and toolConfig belongs to the Converse API.

subjective.question: Explain the tool-calling loop step by step, as you would to a junior developer.
subjective.answer: First, I send the model the conversation and the list of tool definitions. The model replies in one of two ways: a final text answer, or a structured request to call one or more tools. I check the stop signal for this, such as stop_reason 'tool_use' on Anthropic or finish_reason 'tool_calls' on OpenAI. If tools were requested, I read each call's ID, name and arguments. Then I validate the arguments and run the real function in my own code. Next, I append the assistant's tool-call turn to the history, followed by one result per call, each linked by its ID. Then I call the model again. This repeats until the model gives a final answer or I reach my iteration cap. The key idea is that the model only decides. My application executes, and it also owns state, safety and limits.
keyPoints: Send messages plus tool definitions
Check the stop reason for a tool request
Execute the tool in application code, never in the model
Return results linked by call ID, then call the model again
Stop on a final answer or when the iteration cap is reached

subjective.question: What makes a good tool name, description and input schema? Give an example for a weather tool.
subjective.answer: The model chooses tools mainly from the name and description, so they must be clear and specific. The name should be a short, verb-led identifier, such as get_current_weather. The description should say what the tool does, when to use it, when not to use it, and what it returns. For example: 'Get current temperature and conditions for a city. Use for present weather only, not forecasts. Returns Celsius.' The input schema uses JSON Schema: type 'object', with properties such as city (string, with a description like 'City name, e.g. Mumbai') and units (string with an enum of 'celsius' and 'fahrenheit'). Mark only the truly needed fields as required. Enums and good field descriptions cut down on invalid arguments. I also avoid having two tools with overlapping purposes, because that confuses tool selection.
keyPoints: The description drives tool selection, so say when and when not to use it
Use a clear, action-oriented name
JSON Schema object with properties and required
Enums and field descriptions reduce bad arguments
Avoid tools whose purposes overlap

subjective.question: Why do tool calls carry an ID, and what goes wrong if you mismatch it?
subjective.answer: Every tool request from the model has a unique ID, such as a tool_use id on Anthropic, a tool_call id on OpenAI, or toolUseId on Bedrock. When I return a result, I attach that same ID: tool_use_id, tool_call_id or toolUseId. The ID pairs each result with the call that produced it. This matters most with parallel calls. If the model asks for weather in Delhi and in Chennai, the IDs tell it which temperature belongs to which city. If I drop an ID, reuse one, or return a result for an ID that does not exist, the APIs usually reject the request with a validation error. Even when no error is raised, wrong pairing makes the model reason over the wrong data. So my loop should keep the IDs exactly as received and return exactly one result per call.
keyPoints: Each call has a unique ID that the result must echo
The ID field name differs per provider
Essential for pairing results correctly in parallel calls
Mismatches cause API errors or wrong reasoning
Return exactly one result per call

subjective.question: Describe how you would write a tool-calling loop by hand, without a framework, for a weather tool and a calculator tool.
subjective.answer: I define two tool schemas, get_weather(city) and calculate(expression), and a dispatch dictionary that maps each tool name to a Python function. The loop runs for at most MAX_STEPS iterations. In each step I call the model with the messages and tools. If the stop reason is not a tool call, I return the text answer. Otherwise I append the assistant turn unchanged, then go through every tool call. For each call, I look up the function by name, parse and validate the arguments, and run the function inside try/except. I collect a result with the matching ID, marking it as an error if something failed. I append all the results in one turn and continue the loop. If MAX_STEPS runs out, I return a polite fallback. For the calculator, I use a safe expression parser rather than eval. I also log every step, so I can debug and measure latency and cost.
keyPoints: Tool schemas plus a name-to-function dispatch map
Bounded loop that checks the stop reason
Keep the assistant turn, run each call, return results by ID
Wrap tool execution with try/except and report errors as results
Iteration cap, safe calculator, logging

subjective.question: What are parallel tool calls, and when might you disable them?
subjective.answer: Parallel tool calling means the model asks for several independent tool calls in a single turn, for example getting the weather for three cities at once. My application can run them at the same time, using threads or async, and return all the results together. This cuts the number of model round trips and the total latency. I would disable parallel calls, or set them to one call at a time, when the calls depend on each other. An example is when the second call needs an ID returned by the first. I would also disable them when the tools have side effects that must happen in order, such as payments or writes, or when a rate-limited backend cannot handle bursts. OpenAI has a parallel_tool_calls parameter, and Anthropic has disable_parallel_tool_use under tool_choice. Even with parallelism on, every call still needs its own result, matched by its ID.
keyPoints: Several independent calls in one turn
Run them concurrently to cut round trips and latency
Disable for dependent or ordered side-effect calls, or for rate limits
Provider settings: parallel_tool_calls, disable_parallel_tool_use
Every call still needs its own ID-matched result

subjective.question: Explain the idea of 'tool errors as observations'. How do Anthropic and Bedrock let you signal an error?
subjective.answer: When a tool fails, because of an invalid city, a timeout or division by zero, I do not crash the loop. I catch the exception and send a tool result that describes the failure in plain language, for example 'City not found. Try the official city name.' The model treats this like any other observation. It can fix its arguments, try a different tool or explain the problem to the user. This makes agents much more robust. Anthropic supports an is_error flag on the tool_result block. The Bedrock Converse API supports a status of 'error' on the toolResult block. Error messages should be useful but safe: no stack traces, secrets or internal hostnames. I still count these errors against my iteration cap, so a tool that keeps failing cannot trap the model in a retry loop.
keyPoints: Catch exceptions and return them as tool results
The model can self-correct or inform the user
Anthropic is_error; Bedrock status 'error'
Keep messages actionable but free of secrets
Repeated failures still count toward the iteration cap

subjective.question: Why must a hand-written agent loop have a maximum iteration limit? What other safeguards would you add?
subjective.answer: A model can get stuck calling tools again and again. Common causes are a tool that keeps returning unhelpful results, ambiguous instructions, or the model looping between two tools. Without a cap, this burns tokens, API quota and money, and the user waits forever. So I set a maximum number of iterations, and when it is reached I return a graceful fallback or hand over to a human. Other safeguards I would add: a timeout on each tool call, an overall wall-clock and token or cost budget per request, and detection of repeated identical calls. I would validate arguments against the schema before running a tool. For destructive actions, I would require human confirmation. I would also use logging and tracing, so I can see why a run hit the cap and improve the prompts or tool descriptions.
keyPoints: Prevents infinite cycles and runaway cost
Return a graceful fallback when the cap is reached
Per-tool timeouts plus overall time and cost budgets
Detect repeated calls and validate arguments
Human approval for risky actions; trace runs

subjective.question: Explain the main tool_choice options and give a real use case for each.
subjective.answer: tool_choice controls whether and how the model uses tools. 'auto' is the default: the model decides between answering in text and calling a tool. I use it in a general assistant. 'none' blocks tool calls. It is useful for a final summarisation turn, or when I want plain text while still sending the tool list. 'required' on OpenAI, or 'any' on Anthropic, forces some tool call but lets the model choose which one. That suits a router step where every request must go to a tool. Forcing one named tool, such as {type:'tool', name:'extract_invoice'} on Anthropic or a named function on OpenAI, is ideal for structured extraction, where I treat the tool's schema as an output format. Bedrock Converse has similar auto, any and tool choices in toolConfig.toolChoice. Forcing a tool reduces flexibility, so I use it only when the flow truly requires it.
keyPoints: auto: the model decides
none: no tool calls
required/any: must call some tool
Named tool: forced, useful for structured output
Bedrock offers similar options in toolChoice

subjective.question: Compare the tool-calling message formats of Anthropic, OpenAI and the Bedrock Converse API.
subjective.answer: The loop is the same on all three, but the field names differ. On Anthropic, tools have name, description and input_schema. The response has stop_reason 'tool_use' and content blocks of type tool_use with id, name and input, where input is already a parsed object. Results go back in a user message as tool_result blocks with tool_use_id and an optional is_error. On OpenAI Chat Completions, tools are {type:'function', function:{name, description, parameters}}. The assistant message has tool_calls, and function.arguments is a JSON string I must parse. Each result is a separate message with role 'tool' and tool_call_id. On Bedrock Converse, tools sit in toolConfig.tools[].toolSpec with inputSchema.json. stopReason is 'tool_use', the content has toolUse blocks with toolUseId, and results are toolResult blocks in a user message, with an optional status of 'error'. A small adapter layer lets one loop support all three.
keyPoints: Anthropic: input_schema, tool_use blocks, tool_result with tool_use_id
OpenAI: parameters, arguments as a JSON string, role 'tool' with tool_call_id
Bedrock: toolConfig.toolSpec, toolUse/toolResult, status 'error'
Same loop, different field names
An adapter layer hides the differences

subjective.question: What is the Model Context Protocol, and what problem does it solve?
subjective.answer: The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Without it, every app writes custom integration code for every service, which gives N applications times M integrations. MCP defines one protocol instead. A service is wrapped once as an MCP server, and any MCP-capable host, such as an IDE, a desktop assistant or a custom agent, can use it through an MCP client. The roles are host (the AI application), client (one connection inside the host) and server (exposes capabilities). Messages use JSON-RPC 2.0. A session starts with an initialize handshake, where the two sides agree on capabilities, and then the client can call methods such as tools/list and tools/call. MCP does not replace model tool calling. The host still converts MCP tools into the model's tool format and runs the usual loop.
keyPoints: Open standard that solves the N×M integration problem
Host, client and server roles
JSON-RPC 2.0 with an initialize handshake
tools/list and tools/call
Works alongside the model's own tool-calling loop

subjective.question: Describe the MCP primitives and who typically controls each one.
subjective.answer: MCP servers expose three main primitives. Tools are executable functions with a name, description and JSON Schema input. The model decides when to call them, so they are model-controlled, and the host should keep a human in the loop for risky actions. Resources are data, such as files, database records or documents, identified by URIs and read with methods like resources/read. The application usually decides which resources to attach as context. Prompts are reusable templates or workflows, often shown to users as commands, so they are mainly user-controlled. On the client side, there are also capabilities that servers can request. Sampling lets a server ask the client's model for a completion. Roots tell the server which filesystem boundaries it may work in. Elicitation lets a server ask the user for more input. Choosing the right primitive keeps a design clean: actions are tools, context is resources, templates are prompts.
keyPoints: Tools: model-controlled actions
Resources: application-controlled context data identified by URIs
Prompts: user-controlled templates
Client features: sampling, roots, elicitation
Match the primitive to its purpose

subjective.question: Compare the MCP stdio and Streamable HTTP transports. What security points matter for each?
subjective.answer: With stdio, the host launches the MCP server as a local subprocess and exchanges JSON-RPC messages over standard input and output. It is simple and fast, and it suits local tools such as a filesystem or git server. The main risk is that the server runs with the user's local permissions. So I only install trusted servers, and I limit the folders and commands they can reach. Streamable HTTP is the standard remote transport. The client sends JSON-RPC over HTTP POST to a single endpoint, and the server can stream responses back. It replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport in the 2025 spec. For remote servers, I need proper authentication and authorisation (the spec describes an OAuth-based flow), TLS, and validation of the Origin header to block DNS rebinding. A local HTTP server should bind only to localhost. On both transports, I treat tool descriptions and outputs as untrusted input, because of prompt-injection risk.
keyPoints: stdio: local subprocess, standard input and output
Streamable HTTP: remote, single endpoint, replaced HTTP+SSE in 2025
Remote needs authentication, TLS and Origin checks
Local servers run with user permissions, so use least privilege
Treat tool outputs as untrusted (prompt injection)

subjective.question: What exactly does a framework's agent loop do for you? Answer as if this were the checkpoint for this week.
subjective.answer: Having built the loop by hand, I can list what a framework such as smolagents or LangGraph, or a managed service such as Bedrock Agents, automates. It turns my functions into schemas; smolagents' @tool, for example, reads type hints and the docstring's Args section. It calls the model, detects tool requests and parses the arguments, including turning OpenAI's JSON string into an object. It dispatches each call to the right function, runs parallel calls, and pairs results with call IDs. It catches exceptions and feeds them back as observations. It keeps the message history or memory, enforces a maximum number of steps, and often adds retries, streaming, tracing and provider adapters. Nothing in it is magic. When an agent misbehaves, I know where to look: a poor tool description, a bad schema, a missing error result, or the step limit.
keyPoints: Schema generation from code
Call the model, detect tool requests, parse arguments
Dispatch calls, run them in parallel, pair IDs
Error handling, history and a step cap
Tracing and provider adapters, which helps debugging

subjective.question: Your calculator tool receives an 'expression' string from the model. How do you implement it safely?
subjective.answer: I never pass model-generated text to Python's eval or exec, because the arguments are untrusted. A prompt injection in the user input or in a document could make the model send code that deletes files or leaks secrets. Instead, I parse the expression with a safe evaluator. For example, I can walk Python's ast and allow only number nodes and the operators +, -, *, /, ** and parentheses, or I can use a math-expression library. Even better, I can design a structured schema, such as operation (an enum of add, subtract, multiply, divide) plus a and b as numbers, so there is little to parse. I validate the arguments against the schema, limit input length and exponent size to avoid resource exhaustion, and handle division by zero by returning an error result rather than crashing. The general lesson: tool inputs come from the model, so validate them like any external input.
keyPoints: Never eval or exec model output
Use an AST whitelist or a structured enum schema
Validate against the schema; limit size and exponents
Return errors such as division by zero as tool results
Treat model arguments as untrusted input

subjective.question: On AWS, when would you choose the Bedrock Converse API with your own tool loop, and when would you choose Bedrock Agents with action groups?
subjective.answer: With the Converse API, I define tools in toolConfig, check for stopReason 'tool_use', run the tools myself and return toolResult blocks. I own the loop, so I get full control over the orchestration, the error handling, the iteration caps and the choice of model. This suits custom agent logic or code that must be portable across providers. Bedrock Agents is a managed option. I describe tools as action groups, using an OpenAPI schema or function details, and they are usually fulfilled by a Lambda function. The service runs the orchestration, keeps session state, and can connect knowledge bases and guardrails. That suits teams that want less code and native AWS integration, and accept less control over each step. There is also a return-control option, where the agent hands the tool call back to my application instead of calling Lambda. For the exam, remember: Converse means toolSpec and toolResult, while Agents means action groups, OpenAPI or function details, and Lambda.
keyPoints: Converse: you own the loop and have full control
Agents: managed orchestration and session state
Action groups: OpenAPI schema or function details, usually Lambda
Return control hands tool execution back to the app
Trade-off between control and managed convenience

steps.overview: This step teaches the core patterns behind agent systems: Andrew Ng's four agentic design patterns, the ReAct and plan-and-execute loops, and Anthropic's workflow patterns such as routing and orchestrator–workers. Every exam on this path expects you to choose the right pattern for a scenario. You must also be able to explain when a fixed workflow is cheaper, safer and more reliable than a fully autonomous agent.
objectives: Explain the four agentic design patterns (reflection, tool use, planning, multi-agent collaboration) and give a use case for each.
Compare ReAct and plan-and-execute loops, and choose between them for a given task.
Distinguish workflows (code-defined steps) from agents (model-directed steps), and justify when a fixed workflow is the better choice.
Apply routing, parallelisation, orchestrator–workers and evaluator–optimiser to real scenarios.
Build a research agent that plans, searches and critiques its own report, with an iteration cap.

concepts.explanation: The model reviews its own output, or another model reviews it, and then revises it. Well-known research examples are Self-Refine and Reflexion. Reflection works best when you can state clear critique criteria, such as missing citations, factual errors or failing tests. It costs extra LLM calls, so you should cap the number of rounds.

The model calls external functions such as search, code execution, databases or APIs. It does this by emitting a structured call (usually JSON matching a schema) that your code runs. The tool result is fed back into the context. Good tool names, descriptions and parameter schemas matter as much as the prompt does.

The model breaks a goal into ordered sub-tasks before or while acting. Plans can be static (made once) or dynamic (revised after each observation). Planning helps with multi-step goals, but plans made by the model are less predictable than steps you hard-code.

Several specialised agents work together, each with its own role, prompt and tools. Examples include a researcher, a writer and a critic, or a supervisor that delegates to sub-agents. It helps with separation of concerns and with parallel work. The cost is more tokens, more latency and harder debugging. Amazon Bedrock supports this natively through multi-agent collaboration, using supervisor and supervisor-with-routing modes.

ReAct comes from Yao et al., 2022. The agent interleaves Thought → Action → Observation in a loop until it produces a final answer. Each step reasons about the latest observation, so the agent adapts well to surprises. Its weaknesses are that it can wander, repeat tool calls or loop without end. Always set a maximum number of steps.

A planner LLM writes the full multi-step plan first. An executor then carries out each step, often using a cheaper model or plain tool calls. A replanner can update the plan after results come in. Compared with ReAct, it uses fewer calls to the expensive model and is easier to audit. However, it adapts less well between steps.

In a workflow, LLMs and tools are linked through predefined code paths, so your code decides the steps. In an agent, the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use, so the model decides the steps. Anthropic's guidance is to find the simplest solution first. Add agentic autonomy only when it measurably improves results, because agents trade latency and cost for flexibility.

Routing classifies an input and sends it to a specialised prompt, model or handler. For example, simple queries can go to a small model and hard ones to a large model. Parallelisation runs LLM calls at the same time in one of two forms. In sectioning, independent sub-tasks run side by side. In voting, the same task runs several times and the results are aggregated for confidence.

A central orchestrator LLM decides at run time which sub-tasks are needed and sends them to worker LLMs. It then combines their results. The key difference from parallelisation is that the sub-tasks are not known in advance. Typical uses are coding changes across an unknown number of files, or research across unknown sources.

One LLM generates a response and a second LLM evaluates it against criteria and gives feedback, in a loop. This is reflection packaged as a workflow. Use it when clear evaluation criteria exist and iterative refinement measurably improves quality, for example in translation, writing or code that must pass tests.

keyFacts: The four agentic design patterns, as taught in Andrew Ng's Agentic AI course, are: reflection, tool use, planning and multi-agent collaboration.

Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' workflow patterns are: prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation (sectioning and voting), orchestrator–workers and evaluator–optimiser. The building block for all of them is the augmented LLM, meaning an LLM with retrieval, tools and memory.
The ReAct loop order is Thought → Action → Observation, repeated until the agent gives a final answer.
Decision rule: if the steps are known and stable, use a workflow. If the steps cannot be predicted in advance, use an agent.
Orchestrator–workers suits sub-tasks that are discovered at run time. Parallelisation suits sub-tasks that are known in advance.
Evaluator–optimiser only pays off when the evaluation criteria are clear and the feedback actually improves the output.
Every agent loop needs guardrails: a maximum number of iterations or steps, timeouts, a token or cost budget, and a stopping condition.
In Hugging Face smolagents, CodeAgent writes its actions as Python code, while ToolCallingAgent emits JSON tool calls. Both follow a ReAct-style multi-step loop.
Amazon Bedrock Agents orchestrate with a ReAct-style reasoning loop by default. Bedrock multi-agent collaboration uses a supervisor agent that coordinates collaborator agents.

example.caption: Research agent: plan, then search each step, then draft, then critique-and-revise with a capped reflection loop. Replace search() with a real tool such as Tavily, Serper or a RAG retriever.
example.code:
import json
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
MODEL = "your-model-id"  # set to a current Claude model

def llm(prompt: str) -> str:
    r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1500,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return r.content[0].text

def search(query: str) -> str:
    return f"[stub results for: {query}]"  # plug in a real search API

def research(question: str, max_rounds: int = 2) -> str:
    plan = json.loads(llm(f"Return ONLY a JSON list of 3-5 search queries to answer: {question}"))
    notes = [f"Q: {q}\n{search(q)}" for q in plan]          # execute the plan
    report = llm(f"Write a cited report on '{question}' using only these notes:\n" + "\n".join(notes))
    for _ in range(max_rounds):                                 # reflection, capped
        critique = llm("Critique this report for unsupported claims, gaps and missing citations. "
                       f"Reply APPROVED if none.\n\n{report}")
        if "APPROVED" in critique:
            break
        report = llm(f"Revise the report to fix these issues:\n{critique}\n\nReport:\n{report}")
    return report

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(research("How do UPI transaction volumes compare across 2023-2025?"))

pitfalls: Choosing a fully autonomous agent for a task with fixed, known steps, such as invoice extraction followed by validation and then posting. A prompt chain or workflow is cheaper, faster, easier to test and easier to audit. Exams often reward this answer.
Running reflection or ReAct loops with no iteration cap or stop condition. This causes infinite loops, repeated tool calls and runaway token costs.
Confusing orchestrator–workers with parallelisation. If the sub-tasks are fixed in advance, it is parallelisation. If the LLM decides them at run time, it is orchestrator–workers.

Letting the same prompt both generate and judge the output with vague criteria. This gives rubber-stamp critiques. Give the evaluator a concrete rubric, and ground it in tool results or tests where possible.
Adding multi-agent setups too early. Every extra agent adds latency, cost and failure points. Start with one augmented LLM and split it only when you have a clear specialisation benefit.
Writing poor tool descriptions or loose schemas. The model then picks the wrong tool or passes bad arguments. Treat tool definitions as part of prompt engineering.

workflow.title: Choosing and building the right agent pattern

steps.label: Try a single LLM call
steps.detail: Start with one augmented LLM call using retrieval and examples, and measure quality on a small evaluation set.

steps.label: Fixed steps? Use a workflow
steps.detail: If the task breaks into known steps, use prompt chaining, routing or parallelisation in code.

steps.label: Unknown steps? Add planning
steps.detail: If the sub-tasks depend on the input, use plan-and-execute or orchestrator–workers.

steps.label: Unpredictable environment? Use ReAct
steps.detail: When each next step depends on the last observation, let the model run a Thought–Action–Observation loop with tools.

steps.label: Add reflection with criteria
steps.detail: Wrap the output in an evaluator–optimiser loop with a clear rubric and a maximum number of rounds.

steps.label: Set guardrails and budgets
steps.detail: Enforce step limits, timeouts, cost caps, input and output guardrails, and human approval for risky actions.

steps.label: Evaluate and simplify
steps.detail: Compare accuracy, latency and cost against the simpler baseline, and remove any complexity that does not pay for itself.

objective.question: Which list matches the four agentic design patterns taught in Andrew Ng's Agentic AI course?
options: Prompt chaining, retrieval, memory, guardrails
ReAct, plan-and-execute, chain-of-thought, self-consistency
Reflection, tool use, planning, multi-agent collaboration
Routing, parallelisation, orchestrator–workers, evaluator–optimiser
